blocks.text: 当监控器失效时该怎么办？首先，定期检查探针，以便第一时间知道它是否失效。然后，按照层级顺序恢复信号：先尝试重新训练探针；如果不行，再尝试让探针变为非线性；如果还不行，就尝试把探针移到不同的层。疑似擦除是最棘手的情况，因为探针失效本身是模糊的：究竟是概念被擦除了，还是探针不够好？在这种情况下，请注意模型必须能够读取不期望的概念才能使用它，因此探针只需要和模型其余部分一样强大即可。9
总结一下：针对模型内部进行训练可能会破坏我们的监控器，但当探针失效时，概念通常是移动了，而不是消失了。我们的理论和实验大体上说明了它去了哪里、为什么去那里，以及哪些探针能再次找到它；我们相信，理论的持续发展将使其对现实场景更具预测力。虽然我们尚未消除退化风险，但我们现在确实更清楚地知道该警惕什么，以及如何维持可监控性。

blocks.text: For example: imagine you’re an AI model being trained to diagnose pneumothorax. You have no idea what that is. blocks.text: The problem is, pneumothorax is a collapsed lung, and the tubes are how it’s treated after it’s already diagnosed. As humans with common sense, we can clearly see that it’s not very useful to diagnose a condition based on whether doctors have already treated it. If we use the model on real patients who haven’t been treated yet, it will fail spectacularly.

blocks.text: Interpretability offers a language to make our training objectives more precise. Models internally represent concepts such as an image’s background, chest drains, agreement with a user, or cheating on a task. If we can identify those concepts and measure how much a model relies on them, we can use that information to guide training when changing the data is too expensive or doesn’t work.

blocks.text: Our paper proposes a framework for mechanistic shaping: using internal representations to directly specify which concepts to rely on and which concepts to express during training. In other words, mechanistic shaping specifies how a model should solve a task, not just whether the model succeeds in training. We call these methods reliance shaping and expression shaping; reliance shaping tells the model “don’t rely on this”, and expression shaping tells the model “don’t do this.”

blocks.text: Although interpretability can be useful for training,1 training against it can degrade our monitors: the model’s representations may come to circumvent the monitor while the targeted behavior persists.2 Much of our paper studies this risk. We characterize, theoretically and empirically, how a model’s internals can change under mechanistic shaping (e.g., regrowing, re-encoding, relocating, erasing), and show how each kind of change affects monitoring. While we haven’t covered every setting and outcome, our results here are encouraging: across our experiments, the concept remained monitorable after shaping, though it often required a retrained probe.

blocks.text: We applied mechanistic shaping while training a model on a dataset of real chest X-rays.5 The images are labeled according to whether the patient had a collapsed lung, but also contain a shortcut: a chest drain, which shows up clearly as a tube on the X-rays. blocks.text: Models are shaped by their training data, and curating that data is a key lever for shaping model behavior. But some undesirable model behaviors emerge during training with no obvious data examples to blame. Blank et al. (2026) found that direct preference optimization (DPO)—a post-training procedure that contrasts good and bad examples—can make the model much more sycophantic, despite less than 1% of training data being visibly sycophantic.7 Since there’s almost nothing to filter, standard data curation barely reduces sycophancy.

We summarize three main takeaways from the theory here, but the paper shows more:

inlines.text: To better understand what can actually happen and why, we studied the simplest, strongest version of mechanistic shaping:
entirely deleting (projecting out) a concept direction
from the model’s representations. We summarize three main takeaways from the theory here, but the paper shows more:
The concept representation starts regrowing immediately.
The original concept direction gets no training signal, but the task still rewards the existence of the concept, so a new concept direction immediately starts to grow somewhere else.
The regrown representation can become entangled with desired concepts.
The new representation of the undesirable concept grows along directions that the model uses for the task, so it can mix with concepts that we
do
want the model to use for decision-making.
Frequent refreshing can train a nonlinear representation of the concept.

Repeatedly refreshing the concept direction that you use for shaping (i.e., refitting the unwanted concept direction) starts a race between regrowing a new linear concept direction and developing a nonlinear code. Eventually, the nonlinear code can win that race. However, the model can represent the concept linearly again at a later layer, and the type of nonlinear encoding takes a predictable form: a second-order product code (Figure 8).

blocks.text: Figure 8. Repeatedly ablating a concept during training can push it into a product code. a. In a toy model, each input data example sits on the floor of the graphic with two concept input values; the point above the floor shows the model’s latent activity along the “product code axis”, colored by the input value of the undesired concept (green is negative, orange is positive). Over the course of training, the latent activity becomes equal to the product of the desired concept and the undesired one. b. As a result, both values of the undesired concept share the same average activity along the latent product code axis, but they tilt in opposite directions, so linear probes cannot separate them, while nonlinear probes can. It looks complex, but we understand its structure exactly.

blocks.text: Can we still monitor the model after mechanistic shaping? As the theory showed, mechanistic shaping puts pressure on the undesired concept inside the model’s representations, and the representations change as a result. Some of these changes can break a pre-existing probe’s ability to pick up on the undesired concept. However, the theory also shows that a broken probe doesn’t necessarily mean the concept can’t be monitored, because a new probe can often take its place.

blocks.text: What should you do when a monitor fails? First, check the probe periodically so you know if it is failing in the first place. Then, follow the hierarchy to recover the signal: first try retraining the probe; if that fails, then try making the probe nonlinear; and if that fails, try moving the probe to a different layer. Suspected erasure is the trickiest case, because a failed probe is ambiguous: did the concept get erased or was the probe not good enough? In this case, note that the model needs to be able to read the undesirable concept in order to use it, so probes only need to be as powerful as the remainder of the model.9

In summary: training against a model’s internals can break our monitors, but when a probe breaks, the concept has usually moved rather than disappeared. Our theory and experiments generally show where it goes, why, and which probes can find it again, and we believe that continued development of the theory will make it even more predictive of real-world scenarios. While we haven’t eliminated the risk of degradation, we do now have a better understanding of what to watch out for and how to maintain monitorability.

inlines.text: Looking forward

blocks.text: Our results show that mechanistic shaping works across modalities and training regimes at small-to-medium scales: confounded vision, medical imaging, DPO post-training, and reward hacking, to name a few. In several of these settings, behavioral objectives alone are ineffective. Mechanistic shaping is a tool for one of the central problems of alignment: specifying how a model solves a task, not just whether it does.

blocks.text: However, training against interpretability signals requires care: the resulting pressure is neither uniform nor benign by default. Training against interpretability signals does change representations; concepts can be re-encoded linearly or nonlinearly, and they can move to other layers. But in every experiment we ran, the targeted concept remained monitorable, and in most cases, our theory helps explain how and why its representation changed.

blocks.text: Much remains open: e.g., exact understanding of all possible neural codes, analytic solutions for deeper networks, and full understanding of frontier-scale training runs. We haven’t answered every question about monitorability, and our experiments only cover small-to-medium settings. But we believe this research direction now has clearer questions and methods, and shows significant promise; we think that continued research working towards real use of these methods—including at frontier scale—will be critical to AI safety and alignment. Overall, we see this as a significant step toward intentionally designing models from the inside, rather than hoping the right reasons emerge from the right outcomes.
